tracks.title: The graph nobody wrote
tracks.text: Lesson eight point six — worlds. A deep dive, under workflows. [curious] The parent lesson ended on one diagram. A workflow with two components compiles into a world that exports a site. True… one breath. But it has the smell of a marketing claim. Compiles… how? Nobody wrote the wire between the two pieces. Nobody declared an interface. Yet the engine gets a typed-looking, deployable thing with a public surface. So either there is a real algorithm under that arrow… or there is a demo-ware trick. This lesson is the algorithm. And the punchline, up front… it is about thirty lines of set arithmetic you can run in your own head.

tracks.title: The graph nobody wrote
tracks.text: First — the graph nobody wrote. Every other orchestrator makes you author the graph by hand. Airflow has you write the whole dependency tree in Python. GitHub Actions makes you spell out a needs line on every job. Bazel wants explicit deps. And then — separately, in a second file that drifts from the first — you write the interface. A WIT world… a protobuf… an OpenAPI spec. Two graphs to keep honest. [sighs] And an agent reviewing your plan can read neither, when one lives in a UI and the other in a sidecar file. Picture a two-row table. Row one — the old tools — and across it… you write the graph by hand, you write the interface separately. Both no. Row two — a world — and across it… edges are matched for you, the surface is computed for you. Both yes. That contrast is the whole page. What if both were computed from the plan you already wrote… and the computation were small enough to hold in your head?

tracks.title: The world
tracks.text: So — the definition. A world is the build plan the kernel emits from a workflow. Components… inferred data-flow edges… computed imports and exports… nested sub-worlds… and a schedule. One JSON object per workflow headline. Deliberately shaped like a WIT world. One workflow in… one world out. And the shape is fixed — seven keys, no more. Name… schedule… imports… exports… components… edges… and workflows. The components are the tasks you wrote. The edges, the imports, the exports — those three are the things you did not write. The kernel works them out. And workflows, the seventh key, holds nested sub-worlds — a world contains worlds. The kernel that emits all this is about five hundred and fifty lines of pure Rust. No host calls… the same wasm in every surface. And tangle… is just one of its six exports. This page is that one export, told properly.

tracks.title: Six words on a begin source line
tracks.text: Next — six words on a begin-source line. A component's whole interface is the header args on its first source block. There are six. First… deps — a comma-split list, like tokio at one point three five, serde at one — what gets compiled in the sandbox. Second… uses — repeatable, a capability the component needs; declare it many times for many capabilities. Third… out — at most one, the named value this component produces. Fourth… in — at most one, the named value it consumes. And here is the deliberate limit — no fan-in. Fifth… persist — a bare flag, no value, opt in to durable state across runs. And sixth… dir — point at a real project directory instead of the inline block. Anything else on that line is silently ignored. The lens is small on purpose. And notice the two single ones — in and out are each at most one. That is not an oversight. It is exactly what makes the edge inference a clean name-match.

tracks.title: Matching out to in
tracks.text: Now — matching out to in. The first half of the inference, and it is almost embarrassingly small. Build a map from each out-name to the component that produces it. Then for every component with an in, look up a producer of that exact name. If one exists… emit an edge, from producer, to consumer. That is the whole step. Take the real Nightly digest workflow. Three components, three languages, written without a single arrow. Read it as speech. A workflow headline, Nightly digest, scheduled Saturday at six in the morning, repeating daily. Under it… Fetch events, a Rust component, that produces events-list. Then… Summarize, a JavaScript component, that consumes events-list and produces summary-string. Then… Send, a Go component, that consumes summary-string. Now watch the graph draw itself. Fetch produces events-list… Summarize consumes a name spelled exactly events-list — edge. Summarize produces summary-string… Send consumes summary-string — edge. Fetch flows to Summarize flows to Send. And the match is whole-string equality on the name. The colon-string half of summary-string is a convention living inside the name… not a parsed type. The matcher sees one opaque string and compares it to another. Fan-out works — one producer can feed many consumers. Fan-in does not — one in, so a component can never join two upstreams.

tracks.title: The surface is the residue
tracks.text: Here is the turn — the surface is the residue. The moment the whole page pivots on. You have the edges. So ask the producer map one more question. Which outputs did nobody consume? Those leftover outputs are, by definition, the world's public surface. [excited] Exports are not declared. They are computed… as the unconsumed outputs. And imports are just as cheap — the sorted union of every component's uses. You never write the interface, because the interface is the dataflow's residue. Now run that rule against the digest. Imports — the three capabilities, sorted. Edges — Fetch to Summarize, Summarize to Send. And exports… empty. An empty list. And that emptiness is information. Every output this workflow produces is consumed inside it. The digest is a closed pipeline whose only effect on the world is the email capability it imports. The plan is telling you, mechanically — this world has no API… only effects. Leave one output loose, wire nothing to it, and that becomes your export… your public surface… without you ever typing the word. Picture two pipelines side by side. The digest — Fetch, Summarize, Send — consumes everything, so its surface is empty, pure effect. And a Transform pipeline — Clean, then Score — that leaves a score value unconsumed at the end. Its surface is exactly that one value, score. Same algorithm. Two verdicts. The author chose neither. The dataflow decided.

tracks.title: Worlds inside worlds
tracks.text: Depth rung — worlds inside worlds. The compiler walks the headline tree. And a workflow headline nested inside another is not a component — it is a sub-world, compiled by the same recursion, its subtree skipped at the parent level. A component child joins this world's list. Anything else is skipped. The whole tree becomes one nested DAG. Read the real example. A Pipeline workflow. Under it… Ingest, which produces raw-bytes. Then a nested Transform workflow, holding two of its own components — Clean, which consumes raw-bytes and produces clean-json… and Score, which consumes clean-json and produces score. Then back at the top level… Publish, which consumes raw-bytes. Now the verified output. The parent Pipeline has two components — Ingest and Publish — one edge, Ingest to Publish on raw-bytes… and exports empty. The nested Transform has Clean and Score, one edge, Clean to Score on clean-json… and exports the score value. The unconsumed value surfaces on the inner world only, because inference is scoped per nesting level. And here is the honest seam. Clean declares it consumes raw-bytes — but no producer of raw-bytes exists inside Transform. So Clean gets no edge. At run time, a sub-workflow receives the original workflow input… not the parent's intermediate value. Cross-boundary dataflow is not edge-wired. This page owns the algorithm. The story of combining workbooks — grafting, surfaces, the flat forest — belongs to the nesting lesson.

tracks.title: The two flags the diagram skips
tracks.text: Next — the two flags the diagram skips. The two header args that change what a component is, rather than how it wires. Both are easy to imagine wrongly. First… persist. A bare flag — Motoko-style orthogonal persistence. Mark a component persist and it opts into durable state across runs. Picture an Agent workflow. Under it… Remember, marked persist, producing a memory value. And Act, consuming that memory. Ask the engine which components survive a redeploy, and it answers with a one-item list — just Remember. But here is the part worth stating plainly, because the intuition is wrong. Persist is not a snapshot of Wasm linear memory. Components are stateless between runs. Persist is the contract that a component checkpoints its state to the VFS… and the VFS is the orthogonal-persistence layer, where freeze and resume copies it and Litestream replicates it. The durable thing is a file… not a frozen heap. Walk the redeploy. Run one — a persist component checkpoints its state to the VFS. The process exits, memory gone either way. Run two, after a redeploy — the VFS restores the state. Without persist… the component just starts clean. Second flag… dir. The escape hatch. Instead of an inline source block, point the component at a real project directory with its own Cargo file or package file. That is Mode two — a full project compiled entirely in the sandbox. The inline path is Mode one — a content-addressed cache, each block keyed by a hash to a built wasm. The plan just records which lane a component uses.

tracks.title: The shape is a confession
tracks.text: Now — the shape is a confession. Why these exact seven keys? Why imports, and exports, and nested workflows — the vocabulary of a WIT world? Because the kernel that emits worlds… is itself a WIT world. And it eats its own constraint. Picture the kernel's own boundary file. A world named oql. Six exports, every one of them string to string. No imports — zero host calls, so it instantiates with no WASI context. And a fault just traps inside Wasmtime. Pure in… pure out. The kernel rides the same Component Model it imposes on user code. No unsafe… no hand-rolled pointer ABI. The same Rust functions link two ways — a native library into the command-line tool, and the wasm Component the runtime embeds. There is no separate wasm version of the logic. So the plan is WIT-shaped because worlds are meant to be WIT worlds. And two proofs the shape is not decoration. First — the conformance demo runs the kernel itself against the engine contract… and the kernel is rejected. It has no run export, so it is correctly not an engine. Worlds are distinct contracts, enforced. Second — the kernel keeps a record of each component's output name. So the upgrade gate can notice when an output type changed. That is the moment the colon-type suffix stops being decoration and becomes load-bearing. Invisible to the edge matcher… decisive at upgrade time.

tracks.title: Who reads a world
tracks.text: So — who reads a world? One plan, many readers. That is the payoff. The same JSON is build instructions, an execution graph, a capability manifest, and an upgrade contract — and each consumer takes the field it needs. Picture the world in the center, fanning out to six. The Package Manager builds the components. Waves runs them in topological order. The Dock grants capabilities from the imports field. Check-upgrade diffs two worlds. Validate pre-flights the plan. And the schedule field just rides along. And the edges-become-pipes story is two real lines. The runner builds a consumer-to-producer map from the world's edges. Then a node's standard input is either its producer's standard output… or, if it has no edge, the workflow input. That is the entire piping story, in two lines. From there — components run in topological waves, each wave the set of steps whose predecessors are done, parallel within a wave, up to eight at once. A component whose language is agent runs the agent loop instead — its source block is the system prompt, its piped input is the task. And the imports field becomes the capability grants the Dock hands out. The org headline is the DAG. No DSL… no board model. The runtime just executes the plan.

tracks.title: Dumb on purpose
tracks.text: Now the honest part — dumb on purpose. And the honesty is the design argument. The inference is deliberately small. And small means sharp edges you should know before they bite. There are five. First… one input per component — no fan-in. A component cannot join two upstreams. Need to merge two producers? Restructure so something upstream emits the combined value. Second… duplicate out is silently last-wins. Two components producing the same name — the map keeps the last one, no warning. So name your outputs apart. Third… names are not types, until upgrade. The matcher sees the name as one opaque string. The type suffix only bites when the upgrade gate compares two worlds. Fourth… sub-world boundaries are not dataflow-wired. A sub-world's component consuming a parent name gets no edge, and at run time the workflow's original input. Fifth… execution is host-piped today, not WIT-composed. The runner composes standard-in and standard-out filters without WIT — and is honest about its tier. Typed in-WASM composition, the wac plug, is the declared upgrade… and it needs WIT-declared components. The WIT shape is ahead of the WIT plumbing… on purpose. And none of this is a hedge. Thirty lines of set arithmetic you can predict by hand… beat a planner you cannot. That trade is the point.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is the type suffix in a name checked? Not by the edge matcher — it compares whole names as opaque strings. The suffix becomes load-bearing exactly once… when the upgrade gate notices a component's output type changed. Can two components produce the same name? They can — and the last one silently wins, no error. So name them apart. Can a component take two inputs? No — a single in, so no joins. Restructure upstream. Fan-out is fine; fan-in is not. Do I ever write a world by hand? Never. A world is compiled output — the org workflow is the source. You write headlines and six header args… the kernel computes the rest. Where does the schedule go? Into the world record — a schedule property becomes a cron field, else a scheduled timestamp becomes an at, repeat, and active. The schedule rides in the world; firing it is the engine's job. And — is this the same world as WIT's world? Same idea, same shape — imports, exports, nested worlds — at the plan level rather than the bytes level, for now. The kernel itself ships as a real WIT world… and the plan is shaped to match, so worlds can someday be wac-plugged without changing the format.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that is worlds. The graph nobody wrote… because nobody had to. Edges are matched, out to in. Imports are a union. And the surface — the exports — is the residue, the outputs nobody consumed. One inversion that turns a plan into a deployable thing… in about thirty lines you can predict. [curious] The way back up is short. This is a deep dive under workflows — lesson eight — where that single compile arrow first appears. And from here, three roads. Tangling, for authoring those header args by hand. Waves, for how the compiled world actually runs. And nesting, for the story of combining workbooks. But start with the parent. The one-diagram version is where this all began.
